_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 580 words, six questions in text order: detail/opinion, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Honest tricks
subtitle: For twenty-six years Peg Holloway has set the Saturday crossword in the Northern Courier. Dan Price met the woman behind the clues.

cards.text: Every Saturday morning, around forty thousand people sit down with a pen, a cup of tea and a puzzle written by a woman they have never met. They know her only as Magpie, the name printed beneath the crossword in the Northern Courier. Many of them write to her, and not always kindly. 'I get complaints that a clue was too easy and complaints that it was impossible,' says Peg Holloway, who has set the puzzle for twenty-six years. 'Often about the same clue, on the same day. I take that as a sign I've got it about right.'
cards.question: How does Peg feel about the different complaints she receives?
choices: They suggest that her puzzles are well balanced.
They make her want to stop setting puzzles.
They show that readers do not understand her clues.
They are less common than they used to be.
cards.highlight: I take that as a sign I've got it about right.
cards.why: When the same clue is called both 'too easy' and 'impossible', she takes it 'as a sign I've got it about right'. Nothing suggests she wants to stop (B) or blames the readers (C).

cards.text: Peg did not intend to become a crossword setter. For most of her working life she planned bus timetables, a job she describes as 'very similar, but with more angry letters'. She started writing puzzles as a hobby and sent one to the Courier after spotting a mistake in its crossword. 'I wasn't applying for anything,' she says. 'I was just showing off.' The editor rang the following week. The previous setter was about to retire, and nobody else had been foolish enough, as Peg puts it, to point out his errors in writing.
cards.question: What can we infer about why the editor contacted Peg?
choices: She had applied for the setter's job.
Her letter showed she had the skills the paper needed.
She had worked for the newspaper before.
The previous setter had recommended her.
cards.highlight: nobody else had been foolish enough, as Peg puts it, to point out his errors in writing
cards.why: Her puzzle and her note about the setter's mistakes arrived just as he was retiring, so the editor saw she could do the job. She says 'I wasn't applying for anything', so A is wrong.

cards.text: A good cryptic clue, Peg explains, is a kind of honest trick. Every clue must contain everything the solver needs, but arranged so that the obvious reading is the wrong one. She writes most of hers while walking her dog along the canal, muttering words under her breath. Neighbours have learnt not to take this personally. Her dog, a nervous spaniel called Biscuit, has never quite got used to it. 'He thinks I'm talking to him,' she says. 'Eight years of hearing things like "horse loses head in storm". No wonder he looks worried.'
cards.question: What does 'this' refer to in 'Neighbours have learnt not to take this personally'?
choices: her dog's nervous behaviour
the tricks hidden in her clues
her muttering words as she walks
her walks along the canal
cards.why: 'This' is the muttering mentioned just before: neighbours might think the strange words are aimed at them. A walk is nothing to take personally, so D is wrong.

cards.text: Her most famous puzzle appeared ten years ago. A reader called Alan had written to say he was going to propose to his girlfriend, a keen solver, and asked whether Peg could help. She hid the question in the grid: read together, the shaded squares spelled out 'Will you marry me, Ruth?' Ruth finished the crossword on a Saturday morning, stared at it, and said yes. The couple now send Peg a card every anniversary. 'It's the only crossword I've ever written,' she says, 'where I knew exactly who would solve it and how they'd feel.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention Alan and Ruth?
choices: to show how difficult Peg's puzzles can be
to explain how Peg met her own husband
to suggest that Peg will write a puzzle for anyone who asks
to show that a crossword can mean a great deal to one reader
cards.highlight: where I knew exactly who would solve it and how they'd feel
cards.why: The proposal shows a crossword reaching one particular person, the only one where Peg 'knew exactly who would solve it and how they'd feel'. It was a single special request, so C goes too far.

cards.text: Recently, Peg has had to defend her work against a new rival. Some readers have started using apps that solve any crossword in seconds, and one wrote to ask why she bothered making the clues so clever if a phone could crack them anyway. Peg is not worried. 'A machine can find the answer,' she says. 'It can't enjoy the penny dropping.' For her, that moment is the whole point: the second when a clue that made no sense suddenly makes perfect sense, and the solver laughs out loud, alone, at the kitchen table.
cards.question: What does Peg mean by 'the penny dropping'?
choices: the cost of buying the newspaper
the moment a solver suddenly understands a clue
the point when a solver gives up on a clue
the discovery of a mistake in a clue
cards.highlight: the second when a clue that made no sense suddenly makes perfect sense
cards.why: She explains it herself: 'the second when a clue that made no sense suddenly makes perfect sense'. A machine finds answers but misses this feeling; the phrase has nothing to do with money (A).

cards.text: Peg has no plans to retire. She has, however, started to wonder who might replace her one day, and she keeps every letter that points out a mistake in her puzzles. There are not many, but she reads each one carefully, sometimes twice, with a red pen in her hand. 'Whoever writes the rudest one,' she says, 'gets a phone call.' As I leave, she hands me a copy of next Saturday's puzzle and tells me there is a clue in it just for me. It takes me three days to find it, and when I do, I laugh out loud, alone, at the kitchen table.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest?
choices: Peg is planning to retire in the near future.
Peg dislikes readers who criticise her work.
Peg may find her successor the same way she was found.
Peg no longer reads the letters she receives.
cards.why: Like the letters in the opening, a complaint can lead somewhere: the writer of 'the rudest one… gets a phone call', just as the editor rang Peg after she pointed out mistakes. She has 'no plans to retire', so A is wrong.
